    Content from An Introduction to nf-core

    Last updated on 2026-10-20 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is nf-core?
    • Why should I use the nf-core framework?
    • How can I list and filter nf-core workflows on the command line?

    Objectives

    • Define nf-core and explain its connection to Nextflow
    • List and explain the six main benefits of using the nf-core framework
    • Find nf-core community-made workflows and modules on the nf-core website
    • List nf-core community-made workflows on the command line using nf-core tools

    What is nf-core?

    Nf-core is a community-led project to develop a set of best-practice workflows scripted using Nextflow workflow management system, as well as a framework for Nextflow workflow development. Nf-core workflows are governed by a set of guidelines, enforced by community code reviews and automatic code testing.

    The core features and key benefits of nf-core

    There are six core features of nf-core that are beneficial to bioinformaticians and computational biologists, whether they be in a government, private sector, or academic setting:

    1. Community (Participate): The developers and users of the nf-core community collaboratively develop best practices, pipelines, and tools. All code is hosted openly on GitHub, and members actively participate in code reviews and discussions on GitHub and Slack.
    2. Guidelines (Develop): An established a set of guidelines lists the requirements and recommendations for pipeline development. This ensures consistency and adherence to best practices across all workflows. The requirements and recommendations include thorough documentation, usage examples, results descriptions, and test data sets.
    3. Portability (Deploy): All nf-core pipelines allow for execution across local machines and cloud platforms, which surmounts the challenge of creating reproducible analyses across different systems. The nf-core guidelines enforce consistent implementation practices through templates, guidelines, and lint tests that ensure all pipelines fully utilize Nextflow’s portability features. Additionally, nf-core requires all pipelines to bundle dependencies in Docker containers, providing static runtime environments. This minimizes issues related to hardware differences, operating systems, and software versions.
    4. Reproduciblity (Deploy): Once stable, nf-core pipelines are given tagged releases on GitHub. Each version is given a number using semantic versioning, and nf-core​ pipelines support the collection of analysis metadata such as pipeline version, software versions, and command and parameter configuration.
    5. Standardization (Develop): To help developers get started with new pipelines, nf-core provides a standardized pipeline template that adheres to all nf-core guidelines, as well as command line tools for pipeline creation. This lowers barriers to development and provides consistent structure across all pipelines, making them easier to learn, use, and develop.
    6. Research Impact (Participate): The nf-core framework increases reliability and reproduciblity of scientific analyses, and it accelerates scientific discoveries through ready-to-use, validated workflows.
    Discussion

    How might the nf-core framework benefit you?

    Take a moment to reflect on the Nextflow workflows you’ve written or worked on. How might the nf-core framework improve the scripting of your workflow(s)? After reflecting, discuss with the people (or person) next to you.

    What are nf-core workflows?

    nf-core workflows are an organized collection of Nextflow scripts, other non-nextflow scripts (written in any language), configuration files, software specifications, and documentation hosted on GitHub. There is usually a single pipeline for a given data and analysis type e.g. There is a single pipeline for assembly and variant calling from viral sequence data, Viralrecon. All nf-core workflows are distributed under the MIT licence, a highly permissive license that requires the inclusion of a copyright and license notice.

    Finding community workflows

    There are two main ways you can find nf-core workflows. You can manually search the workflows page of the nf-core website, found here, or you can use nf-core tools on the command line.

    Finding nf-core workflows online

    As an example, we’ll look at the webpage for nf-core’s demo pipeline.

    Each nf-core pipeline’s webpage contains the following information, organized in tabs:

    1. Introduction - A summary of the pipeline
    2. Usage - Instructions on how to run the pipeline
    3. Parameters - A list of the pipeline’s parameters, which includes a description of the parameter and their default values
    4. Output - A description of the pipeline’s output
    5. Results - An example of the pipeline’s results
    6. Releases - The pipeline’s version history

    Other useful information on a pipeline’s webpage includes commands to clone the pipeline, and links to ask a question about the pipeline on Slack or open an issue using GitHub. Some workflows also feature Youtube Videos on their webpages, which can also be found on this playlist.

    Finding nf-core workflows on the command line using nf-core tools

    What is nf-core tools?

    nf-core provides a suite of helper tools aim to help people run and develop workflows. The nf-core tools package is written in Python and can run from the command line or imported and used within other packages.

    nf-core tools sub-commands

    You can use the --help option to see the range of nf-core tools sub-commands.

    BASH 

    nf-core --help

    Listing available nf-core workflows

    The simplest sub-command is nf-core workflows list, which lists all available nf-core workflows in the nf-core Github repository.

    The output shows the latest version number and when that was released. If the pipeline has been pulled locally using Nextflow, it tells you when that was and whether you have the latest version.

    BASH 

    $ nf-core pipelines list

    If you supply additional keywords after the workflows list sub-command, the listed pipeline will be filtered. Note: that this searches more than just the displayed output, including keywords and description text.

    Finding genome assembly workflows

    1. What nf-core command would you use to list any bacterial genome assembly workflows?
    2. How many genome assembly workflows are there?

    nf-core tool’s subcommands can be listed using nf-core --help

    1. nf-core pipelines list bacterial genome assembly
    2. One, bacass
    Key Points
    • nf-core is a community-led project to develop a set of best-practice workflows built using the Nextflow workflow management system.
    • nf-core is portable, reproducible, and standardized, making it an ideal framework for workflow design
    • The nf-core tool (nf-core) is a suite of helper tools that aims to help people run and develop nf-core workflows.
    • nf-core workflows can be found using nf-core pipelines list, or by checking the nf-core website.

    Content from Running an nf-core pipeline

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I download an nf-core pipeline using nf-core tools?
    • How do I find out what inputs and outputs a pipeline has?

    Objectives

    • Download nf-core pipelines on command line utilizing Nextflow
    • Find the expected inputs and outputs of a pipeline

    In the last episode, we used nf-core tools to search for pipelines. We will now go through the process of downloading and running an nf-core pipeline.

    Downloading nf-core pipelines

    Software requirements for nf-core pipelines

    As we work with nf-core pipelines, we should consider their software dependencies. nf-core pipelines specify these dependencies using Docker, Singularity, or Conda, and Nextflow handles downloading the containers and creating the Conda environments for you. In theory it is possible to run the pipelines with software installed by other methods (e.g. environment modules or manual installation), but this is not recommended. You will not need to manage any of this in this training, because the tools used by our pipelines are already downloaded in your environment.

    Fetching pipeline code with Nextflow

    Unless you are actively developing pipeline code, you should use Nextflow’s built-in functionality to fetch nf-core pipelines. You can use the following command to pull the latest version of a remote workflow from the nf-core GitHub site.

    BASH 

    $ nextflow pull nf-core/<PIPELINE>

    For the best reproducibility, it is good to explicitly reference the pipeline version number that you wish to use with the -revision/-r flag.

    In the example below we are pulling the nf-core/demo pipeline version 1.2.0.

    BASH 

    $ nextflow pull nf-core/demo -revision 1.2.0

    OUTPUT 

    Checking nf-core/demo:1.2.0 ...
 done - revision: 32893afef8 [1.2.0]

    Usage instructions and documentation

    As we discussed in the last episode, you can find general documentation and instructions for Nextflow and nf-core on the nf-core website. Pipeline-specific documentation is bundled with each pipeline in the /docs folder. This can be read either locally, on GitHub, or on the nf-core website.

    Each pipeline has its own webpage at https://nf-co.re/<pipeline_name> e.g. nf-co.re/rnaseq

    In addition to this documentation, each pipeline comes with basic command-line reference. This can be seen by running the pipeline with the parameter --help, for example. The --help option is a quick way to find out what a pipeline needs and where its results go.

    BASH 

    nextflow run -r 1.2.0 nf-core/demo --help

    The help output groups parameters by topic. Look for the Input/output options group, which lists:

      N E X T F L O W   ~  version 26.04.6

Launching `https://github.com/nf-core/demo` [hopeful_mendel] revision: 32893afef8 [1.2.0]


------------------------------------------------------
                                        ,--./,-.
        ___     __   __   __   ___     /,-._.--~'
  |\ | |__  __ /  ` /  \ |__) |__         }  {
  | \| |       \__, \__/ |  \ |___     \`-._,-`-,
                                        `._,._,'
  nf-core/demo 1.2.0
------------------------------------------------------
Typical pipeline command:

  nextflow run nf-core/demo -profile <docker/singularity/.../institute> --input samplesheet.csv --outdir <OUTDIR>


Input/output options
  --input                       [string] Path to a metadata file containing information about the samples in the experiment.
  --outdir                      [string] The output directory where the results will be saved. You have to use absolute paths to storage on Cloud infrastructure.
  --email                       [string] Email address for completion summary.
  --multiqc_title               [string] MultiQC report title. Printed as page header, used for filename if not otherwise specified.

Reference genome options
  --genome                      [string] Name of iGenomes reference.
  --fasta                       [string] Path to FASTA genome file.

Process skipping options
  --skip_trim                   [boolean] Skip trimming fastq files with seqtk

Generic options
  --multiqc_methods_description [string]          Custom MultiQC yaml file containing HTML including a methods description.
  --help                        [boolean, string] Display the help message.
  --help_full                   [boolean]         Display the full detailed help message.
  --show_hidden                 [boolean]         Display hidden parameters in the help message (only works when --help or --help_full are provided).
 !! Hiding 19 param(s), use the `--showHidden` parameter to show them !!
------------------------------------------------------

    Looking at the output from the --help command we can see which parameters important for inputs and outputs and a description of what they are and what the pipeline expects.

    Other parameter groups in the output detail specific parameters that can be used for different parts of the pipeline, for example they can be used for reference genome or tool analysis options.

    Challenge

    Running an nf-core pipeline: Exercise 1

    1. What command would you use to download the ‘nf-core/bacass’ pipeline using nextflow?
    2. What additional flags would you add to your command that would download the specific version of 2.6.0?
    3. What nextflow command would you run that would provide the inputs and outputs of the pipeline?
    1. nextflow pull nf-core/bacass
    2. nextflow pull nf-core/bacass -revision 2.6.0
    3. nextflow run nf-core/bacass --help
    Key Points
    • The nf-core tools (nf-core) is a suite of helper tools that aims to help people run and develop nf-core pipelines.
    • nf-core pipelines can be downloaded with nextflow pull nf-core/<pipeline>, and a specific version can be downloaded with -revision/-r flag.
    • You can use the nextflow run nf-core/<pipeline> --help syntax to view the input an outputs of a nf-core workflow.
